Distance-Constrained Unlabeled Multi-Agent Pathfinding

Takahiro Suzuki Affiliation: Tohoku University Affiliation: National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST) Email: takahiro.suzuki.q4@dc.tohoku.ac.jp    Yuma Tamura Affiliation: Tohoku University Email: tamura@tohoku.ac.jp    Keisuke Okumura Affiliation: National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST) Email: okumura.k@aist.go.jp
Abstract

We study a graph pathfinding problem Distance-rr Independent Unlabeled Multi-Agent Pathfinding, finding a set of collision-free paths between two sets where agents must stay at pairwise distance at least r+1r+1 at all times. This additional constraint, generalizing collision modeling for classical MAPF, targets aspects of real-world multi-agent coordination. This additional distance constraint makes feasibility (i.e., whether a solution exists) 𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{PSPACE}-complete, in contrast to standard (unlabeled) MAPF, where it can be decided in polynomial time. We address the challenge via two complementary approaches: (i) reduction-based optimal algorithms with a feasibility-preserving compression procedure, and (ii) a configuration generator-based search. Despite the hardness, empirical results show that our algorithm can handle hundreds of agents in a practical timeframe.

1 Introduction

Research on Multi-Agent Pathfinding (MAPF) has attracted considerable attention in the last decade, driven by the growing demand for modern multi-robot systems. MAPF aims to find a set of paths (a plan) from the initial point to the target for given agents, without collisions at every time. In response to diverse requirements and constraints arising in practical settings, many variants of MAPF have been proposed mapf:stern19; one of them is the unlabeled (anonymous) version of MAPF, in which the agents are identical and a collision is defined as multiple agents simultaneously occupying the same vertex. This problem naturally arises in the scenario of homogeneous robots such as warehouse transport mapf:MaK16, where we need to solve an integrated joint problem that optimizes goal assignment and path planning.

Although MAPF has been widely studied, it often simplifies a collision by ignoring geometric interference, which hinders its direct application. For example, we need to address the agents that occupy more than one grid cell (for real-world deployment lamapf:Lehoux24), safety margins (for drone planning drone:honig17), and delay tolerance (for robust execution mapf:Atzmon20). These issues motivate a formulation that goes beyond the standard one.

These extensions can be naturally abstracted to a single distance constraint: any pair of agents comes within a distance rr on a graph. Hence, a feasible placement of agents corresponds to a distance-rr independent set, which has been actively studied in the context of graph theory and graph algorithms. We introduce an extension of unlabeled MAPF; given two vertex subsets, Distance-rr Independent Unlabeled Multi-Agent Pathfinding (rrIUMAPF in short) aims to find a plan between them while keeping the placements distance-rr independent at every time.

Despite the case r=0r=0 has been studied as Unlabeled MAPF mapf:Yu12, this generalization remains largely under-explored; no algorithm applies to general r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N}, while an optimal polynomial-time algorithm is known for r=0r=0. Moreover, prior work reconf:Kristan25 shows the 𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{PSPACE}-completeness for determining feasibility when r=1r=1. 𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{PSPACE}-completeness reveals not only that the problem is unlikely to be solved in polynomial time, but also that some instances have plans with super-polynomial makespan, i.e., feasibility can depend on extremely long-horizon coordination rather than on locally improving moves.

Although no general algorithm is known, rrIUMAPF remains practically motivated and poses a nontrivial algorithmic challenge. To this end, we propose two approaches to tackle rrIUMAPF, respectively following common practice in MAPF: algorithms based on reduction, and configuration generator, which is a function that computes the next placements of the agents from the current ones.

1.1 Our contribution

  1. 1.

    To guarantee the plan quality, we present a reduction to Integer Linear Programming (ILP), and an optimal algorithm based on the reduction. Furthermore, we give a feasibility-preserving compression that works well when the number of agents is small. However, the empirical result reveals the limitation of scalability.

  2. 2.

    To handle large instances, we propose a configuration generator IU-PIBT and search algorithm IU-LaCAM, which is an analogue to PIBT mapf:PIBT and LaCAM MAPF:lacam23 for MAPF. IU-PIBT rapidly computes the next configuration, but its rule-based nature tends to get stuck. IU-LaCAM resolves this issue by adding a search following LaCAM and a livelock detection technique to IU-PIBT, thereby quickly solving large-scale benchmark instances.

The former provides an approach when the plan quality is required, whereas the latter offers a method for handling a large swarm of agents. Together, we establish complementary schemes for rrIUMAPF and enable systematic study of it beyond classical Unlabeled MAPF. In what follows, we present a formulation, related work, algorithms, and evaluations for both approaches in order. All the proofs of the claims are omitted in the appendix.

2 Preliminaries

Notation.

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a simple, undirected, and finite connected graph. For a pair of vertices u,v∈Vu,v\in V, we define dist⁡(u,v)\operatorname*{\textsf{dist}}(u,v) as the length (i.e., number of edges) of the shortest path between uu and vv. For a vertex v∈Vv\in V, the closed neighborhood is N​[v]={w∈V∣v​w∈E}∪{v}N[v]=\{w\in V\mid vw\in E\}\cup\{v\}, and its degree is deg​(v)=|N​[v]|−1\textsf{deg}(v)=|N[v]|-1. We extend the notation; let Nr​[v]N_{r}[v] be a set of vertices uu such that dist⁡(u,v)≤r\operatorname*{\textsf{dist}}(u,v)\leq r for an integer r≥0r\geq 0. We define Δ≔maxv∈V⁡deg​(v)\Delta\coloneqq\max_{v\in V}\textsf{deg}(v) and Δr≔maxv∈V⁡|Nr​[v]|\Delta_{r}\coloneqq\max_{v\in V}|N_{r}[v]|. For a vertex set V′⊆VV^{\prime}\subseteq V, the neighborhood is N​[V′]=⋃v∈V′N​[v]N[V^{\prime}]=\bigcup_{v\in V^{\prime}}N[v]. We define nextr​(s,t)=arg​minv∈N​[nextr−1​(s,t)]⁡dist⁡(v,t)\textsf{next}^{r}(s,t)=\operatorname*{arg\min}_{v\in N[\textsf{next}^{r-1}(s,t)]}\operatorname*{\textsf{dist}}(v,t), and next0​(s,t)=s\textsf{next}^{0}(s,t)=s. We assume that arg​min\operatorname*{arg\min} deterministically returns exactly one vertex. We use a notation for a set of continuous integers: let [i,j][i,j] be a set {i,i+1,…,j−1,j}\{i,i+1,\dots,j-1,j\} for i≤ji\leq j.

Problem Definition.

Let GG be a graph and A=[1,n]A=[1,n] be a set of nn agents. A configuration 𝒬=(q1,…,qn)∈Vn\mathcal{Q}=(q_{1},\dots,q_{n})\in V^{n} is an assignment of each agent to a vertex. Although the configuration 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is defined as a list of vertices, we may also refer to it as a (multi-)set of vertices for convenience. A configuration 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is distance-rr independent if there is no pair of agents i,j∈Ai,j\in A such that dist⁡(𝒬​[i],𝒬​[j])≤r\operatorname*{\textsf{dist}}(\mathcal{Q}[i],\mathcal{Q}[j])\leq r.

Given a set of initial and target vertices S,T⊂VS,T\subset V with |S|=|T|=n|S|=|T|=n and a radius r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N}, rrIUMAPF aims to find a finite sequence of configurations Π=[𝒬0,𝒬1,…,𝒬t∗]\Pi=[\mathcal{Q}_{0},\mathcal{Q}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{Q}_{t^{\ast}}], called a plan, where sets 𝒬0\mathcal{Q}_{0} and 𝒬t∗\mathcal{Q}_{t^{\ast}} equals to SS and TT, respectively. Throughout the plan, each agent can move to one of the closed neighbors of the current vertex, provided that every configuration remains distance-rr independent. Formally, a plan Π\Pi from SS to TT in rrIUMAPF holds:

  1. 1.

    ∀k∈[1,t∗],i∈A:𝒬k​[i]∈N​[𝒬k−1​[i]]\forall k\in[1,t^{\ast}],i\in A:\mathcal{Q}_{k}[i]\in N[\mathcal{Q}_{k-1}[i]] (reachability).

  2. 2.

    ∀k∈[0,t∗]:𝒬k\forall k\in[0,t^{\ast}]:\mathcal{Q}_{k} is distance-rr independent.

Note that vertex conflicts and swap conflicts commonly used in MAPF mapf:stern19 can be omitted due to the distance-rr independence of configurations and anonymous setting.

3 Related work

MAPF Extensions.

Numerous MAPF variants move beyond the classical abstraction to capture practical constraints such as extended-body robots and execution uncertainty. Our work offers an alternative approach to accounting for such an extension.

One line of research extends MAPF beyond point agents. Large-agent MAPF has been studied under various collision models, including continuous Euclidean distance constraints lamapf:agafonov25, explicit geometric shapes lamapf:Li19, and adaptations of Conflict-Based Search (CBS) drone:honig17; lamapf:Li19. While these studies are closely related to our setting in that they generalize collision handling, our formulation represents feasible configurations as distance-rr independent sets. This perspective enables the use of graph-theoretic and combinatorial techniques, which we exploit to derive the tractable algorithm presented in Section 5.

In addition, we focus on the unlabeled setting, where generalized collision handling has been largely underexplored. Since unlabeled MAPF often admits more tractable formulations than its labeled counterpart, as reflected in the complexity of makespan optimization mapf:Yu13hard; mapf:Yu12 and in the design of efficient suboptimal algorithms mapf:PIBT; mapf:tswap, developing a planner tailored to the unlabeled setting enables a faster and more scalable approach than directly adapting labeled algorithms with target assignment.

Another line of work relaxes perfect synchrony, considering robust execution under delays mapf:Atzmon20 and time uncertainty safemapf:Shahar21; mapf:otimapp22; a plan of rrIUMAPF is one for unlabeled MAPF that allows delays of at most rr steps.

Reduction-based Approach

translates MAPF into well-known problem and leverage off-the-shelf solvers, e.g., SAT-based approach for MAPF MAPF:surynek16, and flow-based optimal one for unlabeled MAPF mapf:Yu12. One of the advantages is that they can readily provide guarantees: often used when the plan quality is required. We follow this line of work.

Configuration Generator-based Approach

is one of the successful schemes for large-scale, discrete coordination problems mapf:PIBT, as it rapidly generates the successor configuration from the current one and iterates through execution. These algorithms find plans in large instances by localizing the search. Moreover, MAPF:lacam23 (MAPF:lacam23) develops a search algorithm, LaCAM, that leverages a configuration generator, addressing long-horizon tasks that are difficult to handle solely with a configuration generator. Prior works mapf:Fu25; cumapf:suzuki25 show the advantages of this approach for MAPF variants beyond classical formulation (including the anonymity of agents), and these approaches partially inspire our work.

4 Optimal algorithm with ILP

As described in Section 3, several works on MAPF take a reduction-based approach to guarantee the solution quality. In this study, we also adopt a reduction-based approach for rrIUMAPF to perform planning with guaranteed solution quality: we choose ILP as the target of the reduction to handle the distance-rr independence constraint flexibly.

First, we define the Bounded rrIUMAPF: given a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), vertex subsets S,T⊆VS,T\subseteq V, and time bound τ∈ℕ\tau\in\mathbb{N}, it determines whether there is a plan with length at most τ\tau. Let xv,tx_{v,t} be a variable that indicates whether an agent is at v∈Vv\in V at step tt, that is, xv,t=1x_{v,t}=1 when v∈𝒬tv\in\mathcal{Q}_{t}, and xv,t=0x_{v,t}=0 otherwise. Also, fu,v,tf_{u,v,t} represents whether an agent at vertex uu at step tt moves to v∈N​[u]v\in N[u] at step t+1t+1 along u​v∈Euv\in E. Then, the problem can be formulated by ILP as follows.

  1. 1.

    ∀(v,t)∈V×[0,τ]\forall(v,t)\in V\times[0,\tau], xv,t∈[0,1]x_{v,t}\in[0,1].

  2. 2.

    ∀(u,v,t)∈V2×[0,τ]\forall(u,v,t)\in V^{2}\times[0,\tau], fu,v,t∈[0,1]f_{u,v,t}\in[0,1].

  3. 3.

    The initial (or final) configuration 𝒬0\mathcal{Q}_{0} (resp. 𝒬τ\mathcal{Q}_{\tau}) coincides with SS (TT): for v∈Vv\in V, xv,0=1x_{v,0}=1 if v∈Sv\in S (xv,τ=1x_{v,\tau}=1 if v∈Tv\in T), and xv,0=0x_{v,0}=0 (xv,τ=0x_{v,\tau}=0) otherwise.

  4. 4.

    For every step t∈[0,τ−1]t\in[0,\tau-1], exactly xu,tx_{u,t} agents on uu moves to some vertex v∈N​[u]v\in N[u]: ∀u∈V\forall u\in V, ∑v∈N​[u]fu,v,t=xu,t\sum_{v\in N[u]}f_{u,v,t}=x_{u,t}.

  5. 5.

    For every step t∈[1,τ]t\in[1,\tau], exactly xu,tx_{u,t} agents on uu comes from some vertex v∈N​[u]v\in N[u]: ∀u∈V\forall u\in V, ∑v∈N​[u]fv,u,t−1=xu,t\sum_{v\in N[u]}f_{v,u,t-1}=x_{u,t}.

  6. 6.

    For every step t∈[0,τ]t\in[0,\tau], 𝒬t\mathcal{Q}_{t} is distance-rr independent: ∀u,v∈V\forall u,v\in V s.t. dist⁡(u,v)≤r.\operatorname*{\textsf{dist}}(u,v)\leq r. xu,t+xv,t≤1x_{u,t}+x_{v,t}\leq 1.

Condition 6 guarantees distance-rr independence of a configuration: for every pair u,v∈Vu,v\in V with distance at most rr, it holds xu,t=0x_{u,t}=0 or xv,t=0x_{v,t}=0. Then we set an objective as a constant, to check whether there is a satisfying assignment to these constraints. It leads to an optimal algorithm, since the time bound for YES-instances is upper bounded by (|V​(G)|n)\binom{|V(G)|}{n}: the number of vertex subsets with size nn.

5 Compression Algorithm

The above ILP adds O​(|V|2)O(|V|^{2}) constraints per step, even when the number of agents nn is extremely small. However, one might think that if nn is small, a given graph contains redundant vertices that can be contracted while preserving feasibility. Such a reduction results in a more compact ILP instance. In this section, we theoretically demonstrate that such a reduction is possible if Δ\Delta and nn are sufficiently small. Specifically, we develop an algorithm called a kernelization that bounds the size of the reduced graph by a function of Δ\Delta and nn. To this end, we reduce rrIUMAPF to the galactic reconfiguration framework gal:Bartier23. It was recently established to design kenelizations for Token Sliding, which asks whether one can reach a target token placement from an initial one by repeatedly sliding a token to an adjacent vertex while maintaining the placements as an independent set reconf:hearn05. To adapt the framework to rrIUMAPF, we first define notations for the algorithms and the galactic variant. We then present a kernelization for Galactic 1​IUMAPF1{\textsc{IUMAPF}} (GMAPF in short). Finally, we generalize this method to the distance-rr variant.

Kernelization and 𝖥𝖯𝖳\mathsf{FPT} algorithm.

A parameterized problem of a decision problem LL is a set of instances (x,κ)(x,\kappa), where xx is an instance of LL and κ∈ℕ\kappa\in\mathbb{N} is called the parameter of the problem. An algorithm for 𝒫\mathcal{P} is fixed-parameter tractable (𝖥𝖯𝖳\mathsf{FPT}) if the algorithm solves 𝒫\mathcal{P} in h​(k)⋅poly​(|x|)h(k)\cdot\mathrm{poly}(|x|) time for every instance (x,κ)(x,\kappa), where hh is some computable function and |x||x| is the size of xx. Moreover, 𝒫\mathcal{P} admits a kernelization if there is a polynomial-time algorithm that takes an instance (x,κ)(x,\kappa) and outputs another instance (x′,κ′)(x^{\prime},\kappa^{\prime}) (called a kernel) such that (i) xxis a YES-instance of 𝒫\mathcal{P} if and only if x′x^{\prime} is a YES-instance of 𝒫\mathcal{P}, (ii) |x′||x^{\prime}|is bounded from above by f​(κ)f(\kappa), where ff is a computable function, and (iii) κ≥κ′\kappa\geq\kappa^{\prime}. Kernelization immediately yields an 𝖥𝖯𝖳\mathsf{FPT} algorithm via exhaustive search. See para:Cygan15 for more details.

Notation for GMAPF.

For a vertex subset SS of a graph GG, let G​[S]G[S] denote the subgraph induced by SS. A graph GG is connected if there is a path between any two vertices of GG. A component of GG is a maximal connected subgraph. A galactic graph G=(P∪B,E)G=(P\cup B,E) is a graph whose vertex set is the disjoint union of two sets PP (called planets) and BB (called black holes). Recall that, in rrIUMAPF, agents are required to keep each configuration independent; thus, no vertex can be occupied by more than one agent at any time. We relax this constraint so that only agents on the vertices in PP are required to be independent, while each vertex in BB may hold at most nn agents. That is, a black hole b∈Bb\in B behaves as a vertex that absorbs agents located at adjacent vertices. We say that a configuration 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is galactic distance-rr independent if there is no pair i,j∈Ai,j\in A such that 𝒬​[i],𝒬​[j]∈P\mathcal{Q}[i],\mathcal{Q}[j]\in P and distP⁡(𝒬​[i],𝒬​[j])≤r\operatorname*{\textsf{dist}}_{P}(\mathcal{Q}[i],\mathcal{Q}[j])\leq r, where distP⁡(u,v)\operatorname*{\textsf{dist}}_{P}(u,v) for a pair of vertices u,v∈Pu,v\in P is the length of the shortest path in G​[P]G[P] between uu and vv. In particular, a galactic distance-11 independent configuration is simply called a galactic independent configuration. Given a galactic graph GG and two sets of vertices S,T⊆PS,T\subseteq P such that b∉N​[S∪T]b\notin N[S\cup T] for all black hole bb and |S|=|T|=n|S|=|T|=n, Galactic rrIUMAPF asks whether there is a plan Π=[S=𝒬0,𝒬1,…,𝒬t∗=T]\Pi=[S=\mathcal{Q}_{0},\mathcal{Q}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{Q}_{t^{\ast}}=T] satisfying the following two conditions:

  1. 1.

    ∀k∈[1,t∗],∀i∈A:𝒬k​[i]∈N​[𝒬k−1​[i]]\forall k\in[1,t^{\ast}],\forall i\in A:\mathcal{Q}_{k}[i]\in N[\mathcal{Q}_{k-1}[i]].

  2. 2.

    ∀k∈[0,t∗]:𝒬k\forall k\in[0,t^{\ast}]:\mathcal{Q}_{k} is galactic distance-rr independent.

Note that GMAPF generalizes 1​IUMAPF1{\textsc{IUMAPF}}; an instance (G=(V,E),S,T)(G=(V,E),S,T) of 1​IUMAPF1{\textsc{IUMAPF}} can be viewed as an instance (G′=(P∪B,E),S,T)(G^{\prime}=(P\cup B,E),S,T) of GMAPF with P=VP=V and B=∅B=\emptyset.

ILP formulation of GMAPF.

Observe that GMAPF can be reduced to ILP by slightly modifying 1​IUMAPF1{\textsc{IUMAPF}} formulation as follows: Cond. 1: xv,t∈[0,1]x_{v,t}\in[0,1]if v∈Pv\in P, and xv,t∈[0,n]x_{v,t}\in[0,n] otherwise; Cond. 2: fu,v,t∈[0,n]f_{u,v,t}\in[0,n]if u,v∈Bu,v\in B, and otherwise fu,v,t∈[0,1]f_{u,v,t}\in[0,1], and; Cond. 6 galactic independence: ∀u,v∈P\forall u,v\in Ps.t. distP⁡(u,v)≤1.xu,t+xv,t≤1\operatorname*{\textsf{dist}}_{P}(u,v)\leq 1.~x_{u,t}+x_{v,t}\leq 1. By the same discussion as Section 4, we obtain an optimal algorithm for GMAPF; similar for Distance-rr variant.

5.1 Kernelization for GMAPF

Given an instance (G=(P∪B,E),S,T)(G=(P\cup B,E),S,T), we first perform a preprocessing step as follows. For each vertex v∈Pv\in P, we partition the vertices into layers: Li≔{v∈P∣d​(v)=i}L_{i}\coloneq\{v\in P\mid d(v)=i\}, where d​(v)≔mins∈S∪T​distP⁡(s,v)d(v)\coloneq\min_{s\in S\cup T}\operatorname*{\textsf{dist}}_{P}(s,v). Note that every vertex is contained in exactly one layer. Under this preprocessing, our kernelization algorithm repeatedly performs the following two reductions: one is a straightforward rule, and the other generates black holes. For the sake of simplicity, we write VpV_{p} for the set of vertices in the planet that are not adjacent to SS or TT, i.e., P∖(N​[S∪T])P\setminus(N[S\cup T]), and we write Gp=G​[Vp]G_{p}=G[V_{p}].

Reduction rule 1.

If two black holes uu and vv are adjacent, we contract them into a single black hole.

Reduction rule 2.

Let v∈Vpv\in V_{p} be a vertex of a component CC of GpG_{p}. If vv is included in the layer LkL_{k} such that k≥2​n+3k\geq 2n+3, we replace CC with a single black hole bb, and connect bb to every vertex in N​[C]∖CN[C]\setminus C by adding edges.

Our core idea of Reduction rule 2 is that, if there is a vertex vv that is included in LkL_{k} with k>2k>2, then there is a path with k−2k-2 vertices that is not touched by N​[S∪T]N[S\cup T]. If k≥2​n+3k\geq 2n+3 (Figure 1 left), there is an independent set with nn vertices on the path. Moreover, agents placed on vertices in CC can be reassigned to the path without breaking galactic independence (Figure 1 center); CC can absorb nn agents and behave like a black hole. Thus, we contract CC into bb (Figure 1 right).

Lemma 1.

Reduction rules 2 and 1 are both safe, i.e., there is a plan in the graph after reductions if and only if there is a plan in the one before reductions.

The reductions terminate in linear time. Consider an instance (G,S,T)(G,S,T) of GMAPF, where Reduction rules 2 and 1 are iteratively applied until no updates are available. One can observe that every planet pp has its layer less than 2​n+22n+2; otherwise pp is contracted into a black hole. Moreover, the size of BB is bounded by |N​[P]∖P||N[P]\setminus P|. This leads to 1.

Theorem 1.

GMAPF admits a kernel with ΔO​(n)​n\Delta^{O(n)}n vertices.

Moreover, if we are given an induced grid graph, an induced subgraph of the Cartesian product of two paths, the upper bound of |P||P| is much smaller. Note that induced grid graphs are commonly used in empirical evaluation of the MAPF algorithms mapf:stern19.

Theorem 2.

GMAPF admits a kernel with O​(n3)O(n^{3}) vertices when an induced grid graph is given.

Corollary 1.

IUMAPF admits an 𝖥𝖯𝖳\mathsf{FPT} algorithm when parameterized by Δ+n\Delta+n.

Extension to Distance-rr variant.

Recall that our core idea is to find a path of sufficiently long length that can “absorb” nn agents. In the distance-rr variant, an analogous argument holds for a path of length (r+1)​(n+1)−1(r+1)(n+1)-1. Therefore, it suffices to modify Reduction rule 2 to find a vertex with the layer LkL_{k} with k≥(r+1)​(n+1)−1+(r+1)=(r+1)​(n+2)−1k\geq(r+1)(n+1)-1+(r+1)=(r+1)(n+2)-1, ensuring that the path does not touch the distance-rr neighbors of S∪TS\cup T. From the same discussion on 1, the problem admits a kernel of size ΔO​(r​n)​n\Delta^{O(rn)}n.

6 Configuration Generator-Based Algorithm

Although the ILP-based algorithm guarantees solution quality, it has scalability limitations, as we observe in Section 7.1. To complement this limitation, this section proposes a configuration generator-based algorithm IU-LaCAM, scalable for large instances. IU-LaCAM consists of the configuration generator IU-PIBT that supports distance-rr independence and a search scheme LaCAM with tuning for the unlabeled setting. We first present IU-PIBT, and then search.

6.1 Configuration Generator IU-PIBT

IU-PIBT takes the current configuration 𝒬from\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}}, the target TT, and a bijection g:A→Tg:A\to T (used for a target assignment) as input to compute the configuration 𝒬to\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}} and a new bijection g′:A→Tg^{\prime}:A\to T for the next time step. Note that an initial bijection can be obtained by some bipartite matching algorithm (e.g., the Hungarian method) with distance evaluation.

Concept.

IU-PIBT is inspired by rotation-free PIBT mapf:PIBT, which repeatedly performs prioritized one-step planning, i.e., sequentially determining the next location 𝒬to​[i]\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}}[i] of each agent ii in decreasing order of priority. It additionally prevents rotations, namely cyclic moves where agents simultaneously shift along a directed cycle, since it is enabled by the standard abstraction for MAPF. In this paper, IU-PIBT generates 𝒬to\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}} while maintaining distance-rr independence. Moreover, it avoids distance-rr rotations, a sequence of agents (a1,a2,…,ak)(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{k}) such that 𝒬to​[ai]∈Nr​[𝒬from​[ai+1]]\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}}[a_{i}]\in N_{r}[\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}}[a_{i+1}]] for i∈[1,k−1]i\in[1,k-1], and 𝒬to​[ak]∈Nr​[𝒬from​[a1]]\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}}[a_{k}]\in N_{r}[\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}}[a_{1}]]. Further, inspired by the suboptimal unlabeled MAPF work mapf:tswap, it finds a plan by inserting swap and rotation of goal assignment in IU-PIBT.

Algorithm.

Algorithm 1 illustrates IU-PIBT, consisting of (i) top-level procedure (line 3–9), and (ii) recursive function (line 11–24). Blue lines indicate the differences from the original PIBT. Our core is a function IU-PIBT, which determines the next location 𝒬to​[i]\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}}[i] for agent ii with a list SS of agents and a bijection gg, so that dist⁡(𝒬to​[i],𝒬to​[j])>r\operatorname*{\textsf{dist}}(\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}}[i],\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}}[j])>r holds for all agents j≠ij\neq i, and 𝒬from​[j]∉Nr​[𝒬to​[i]]\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}}[j]\notin N_{r}[\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}}[i]] holds for all agents j∈Sj\in S. Here, SS denotes the set of agents waiting for agent ii to move. When attempting to move agent jj to vertex vv, agent ii blocks the move due to the constraint of distance-rr independence. In such a case, we consider moving ii first through a recursive process. By maintaining SS, we prevent distance-rr rotations: if there exists j∈Sj\in S with 𝒬from​[j]∈Nr​[𝒬to​[i]]\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}}[j]\in N_{r}[\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}}[i]], the distance-rr rotation involving ii occurs, and jj cannot move to vv. In other words, IU-PIBT fixes 𝒬to​[j]\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}}[j] for each j∈Sj\in S only if both conditions for ii are satisfied. A step-by-step example of execution is shown in Figure 2.

(i) Top-level procedure. (line 3–9)

Given a configuration 𝒬from\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}}, goals TT, temporal target assignment g:A→Tg:A\to T, IU-PIBT first detects a deadlock starting with i∈Ai\in A, which is a sequence of agents (i=a1,a2,…,aℓ)(i=a_{1},a_{2},...,a_{\ell}) that satisfies nextr+1​(𝒬from​[ak],g​(ak))=𝒬from​[ak+1]\textsf{next}^{r+1}(\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}}[a_{k}],g(a_{k}))=\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}}[a_{k+1}] for k∈[1,ℓ−1]k\in[1,\ell-1], and nextr+1​(𝒬from​[aℓ],g​(aℓ))=𝒬from​[a1]\textsf{next}^{r+1}(\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}}[a_{\ell}],g(a_{\ell}))=\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}}[a_{1}] (see Figure 3 (a) left). If a deadlock is detected, we exchange the targets of agents to eliminate it (Figure 3 (a) right). The detailed implementation is shown in the Appendix. Then IU-PIBT updates the goal priorities based on the assignment gg and the current configuration 𝒬from\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}}. For a goal v∈Tv\in T, if there exists an agent i∈Ai\in A that has arrived at its goal vv (i.e., g​(i)=𝒬from​[i]=vg(i)=\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}}[i]=v), then p′​(v)p^{\prime}(v) is defined as frac​(p​(v))≔p​(v)−⌊p​(v)⌋\textsf{frac}(p(v))\coloneqq p(v)-\lfloor p(v)\rfloor; otherwise, p′​(v)p^{\prime}(v) is set to p​(v)+1p(v)+1. Here, we assume that at step 0, each goal receives a unique decimal p​(v)∈(0,1)p(v)\in(0,1) to break ties. IU-PIBT sorts agents in descending order of p′​(g​(i))p^{\prime}(g(i)) for i∈Ai\in A, and in that order, it calls IU-PIBT for an agent ii with the next location 𝒬to​[i]=⊥\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}}[i]=\bot (means undecided), and determines 𝒬to​[i]\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}}[i] sequentially.

(ii) IU-PIBT. (line 11–24)

Then, IU-PIBT determines the next location for agent ii with a list SS of agents and a temporal target assignment. We enumerate the neighbors, and sort them in ascending order of dist⁡(v,g​(i))\operatorname*{\textsf{dist}}(v,g(i)) for v∈N​[𝒬from​[i]]v\in N[\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}}[i]].

A function IU-PIBT then validates whether moving ii to vv violates the distance-rr independence or causes a distance-rr rotation (line 13–23). Specifically, the move is rejected if there is an agent j≠ij\neq i such that 𝒬to​[j]≠⊥\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}}[j]\neq\bot or 𝒬to​[j]∈Nr​[v]\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}}[j]\in N_{r}[v] (line 14), or there is an agent j∈Sj\in S such that 𝒬from​[j]∈Nr​[v]\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}}[j]\in N_{r}[v] (line 15). Otherwise, IU-PIBT temporarily decides to move ii to vv (line 16). However, there may exist agents j≠ij\neq i whose next location is currently undetermined (𝒬to​[j]=⊥\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}}[j]=\bot), but will later be assigned to a vertex in Nr​[v]N_{r}[v]; this breaks distance-rr independence. To validate whether the agent ii can move vv, IU-PIBT recursively calls IU-PIBT for the agent jj to ask whether jj can move to a vertex v′∉Nr​[v]v^{\prime}\notin N_{r}[v] (line 20). Here, we add ii to a list SS to avoid a distance-rr rotation involving ii. If this recursive call fixes 𝒬to​[j]\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}}[j] to be in Nr​[v]N_{r}[v], then the for-loop of lines 18–21 breaks, and IU-PIBT tries another vertex in N​[𝒬from​[i]]N[\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}}[i]] as the next location 𝒬to​[i]\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}}[i] of agent ii. If ii passes these checks, IU-PIBT fixes the next location 𝒬to​[i]\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}}[i] as the vertex vv and returns VALID. When the for-loop of lines 13–23 fails for all candidates v∈N​[𝒬from​[i]]v\in N[\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}}[i]], it forces ii to stay at 𝒬from​[i]\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}}[i].

Target swapping. (line 17, 23)

As a preprocessing of the recursive call, we additionally perform a temporal target swapping. Given an agent ii and vertex v∈N​[v]v\in N[v], function SWAP​(i,v)\textsc{{SWAP}}(i,v) asks, there is an agent that should swap the goal with ii. Suppose that there is an agent kk (denoted by SWAP​(i,v)\textsc{SWAP}(i,v)) at nextr​(v,g​(i))\textsf{next}^{r}(v,g(i)), and 𝒬from​[k]=g​(k)\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}}[k]=g(k) (Figure 3 (b) middle). Such kk blocks agent ii from reaching its goal. To avoid this, we temporarily swap the goals of these two (line 17). If the recursive call returns VALID (line 22), then the swap is fixed (Figure 3 (b) top). Otherwise (line 23), we revert it by swapping back (Figure 3 (b) bottom). A pseudocode of the function SWAP is provided in the Appendix.

6.2 Theoretical Analysis of IU-PIBT

Now we argue that IU-PIBT is a reasonable configuration generator. In what follows, we present soundness, running time, completeness for 0\mathrm{0}IUMAPF in some restricted cases, and adversarial instance. The discussion of solution quality for r≥1r\geq 1 is omitted due to 𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{PSPACE}-completeness.

Lemma 2.

If 𝒬from\mathcal{Q}^{\text{from}} is distance-rr independent, then 𝒬to\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}} is reachable and a distance-rr independent configuration.

Lemma 3.

IU-PIBT outputs 𝒬to\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}} in Δr​Δ​(r+1)​n+α\Delta_{r}\Delta(r+1)n+\alpha time, where α\alpha denotes the time for resolution of deadlock.

Theorem 3.

IU-PIBT is complete for 0\mathrm{0}IUMAPF, when the given graph has no edge u​v∈Euv\in E such that G​[V∖{u,v}]G[V\setminus\{u,v\}] is not connected.

Adversarial instances.

Since IU-PIBT employs sequential decision for 𝒬to\mathcal{Q}^{\text{to}}, it performs poorly on instances where multiple agents must move simultaneously (see Figure 4 (a)). Furthermore, when a pair of agents attempts to pass each other, they cannot rotate, causing a livelock (see Figure 4 (b)). These examples show that IU-PIBT can fail even on simple local structures. While one may add ad hoc rules to handle these particular cases, obtaining a general scheme that guarantees completeness is unlikely to be simple, since deciding feasibility in rrIUMAPF is 𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤\mathsf{PSPACE}-complete.

6.3 IU-LaCAM

Although IU-PIBT gets stuck when distance-rr rotations are needed, a rotation-free implementation is necessary for the validity of configurations, and it is difficult to overcome this issue with a simple rule-based method. Thus, we employ the LaCAM search and propose IU-LaCAM for rapid planning.

LaCAM MAPF:lacam23 is a well-known complete MAPF solver that utilizes a configuration generator with constraints, which include a subset of agents and their next locations for creating a successor configuration of the current one. LaCAM maintains search states as tuples ⟨𝒬,⟦𝒞⟧⟩\langle\mathcal{Q},\llbracket\mathcal{C}\rrbracket\rangle of a configuration and a list of constraints during the search; if the generator produces a configuration identical to one already generated, it modifies the constraints to induce the generation of a different configuration. Eventually, it tries all possible constraints for every configuration, thereby generating all reachable successors. This guarantees completeness.

It was originally developed for labeled MAPF; however, we can also adapt it to the unlabeled setting by including the target assignment function gg in the search state. A brief pseudocode of LaCAM is in the Appendix. Here, a prior work mapf:lagat25 reports that a livelock detection scheme potentially accelerates the search speed of LaCAM. Inspired by these results, we introduce a similar technique: we detect the livelock described in Section 6.2 and resolve it by reconstructing the target assignment.

A concrete strategy is shown in Algorithm 2, where each search node stores a list ℬ\mathcal{B} of goals that must not be chosen as its goal during assignment for each agent, in addition to 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, ⟦𝒞⟧\llbracket\mathcal{C}\rrbracket, and gg. If a new configuration constructed by IU-PIBT (see the Appendix for pseudocode) is identical to one of the most recent dd (=2=2 in our experiment) configurations and the assignment gg is also identical, then we regard the search as entering a livelock. Then, we detect the set DD of agents that have not reached their goals and whose positions have not changed. For i∈Di\in D, we add each goal g​(i)g(i) to ℬ\mathcal{B} so that its current goal will not be assigned in a new function g′g^{\prime}. If we can compute g′g^{\prime} that avoids ℬ′\mathcal{B}^{\prime}, then we update the stack so that IU-PIBT is called with g′g^{\prime} and reset constraints (line 10).

This target reassignment does not break the completeness of LaCAM, since the number of target reassignments (line 8) is bounded, thus initialization of constraints is bounded.

Theorem 4.

IU-LaCAM is complete for rrIUMAPF.

7 Empirical Evaluation

We evaluate both ILP- and configuration generator-based methods on several maps. These are coded in Python, and the experiments were run on a Mini PC with Intel Core i9-13900H 2.6 GHz2.6\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz} CPU and 32 GB32\text{\,}\mathrm{GB} RAM. For our evaluation, we use the empty-16-16, random-64-64-20, lak303d, and warehouse-10-20-10-2-2 in MAPF benchmarks mapf:stern19. Since the scenario in MAPF benchmarks does not apply to rrIUMAPF, we generate instances by sampling two random distance-rr independent sets (SS and TT), for each map, distance rr, and number of agents nn.

7.1 Evaluation of Exact ILP algorithms

Table 1 shows both the effectiveness and limitations of ILP approach, which uses Gurobi as the ILP solver. We prepare 50 random instances for each setting. On a simple map (empty-16-16), the solver can find an optimal solution within a second, while on a large-scale instance (random-64-64-20), the solver often fails to find a solution, and the number of failed instances increases as nn increases. On large maps, compression can partially mitigate this issue; see random-64-64-20 with n=10n=10. However, this improvement appears only in extremely sparse settings. These results indicate that the scalability of the ILP approach is primarily limited by the growth in the number of variables. In settings where kernelization does not effectively reduce the instance size, IU-LaCAM overcomes this scalability barrier. Indeed, IU-LaCAM achieves at least a 500%500\% speedup on empty-16-16, and a speedup by a factor of roughly 100100 on random-64-64-20 (e.g., n=30n=30 and r=1r=1).

7.2 Large-scale Problem of r≥1r\geq 1

We evaluate the scalability of the configuration generator-based approach LaCAM on large instances. Since our ILP-based algorithm is not scalable to a large-scale setting, we exclude ILP from these experiments. We generate random instances on the large maps random-64-64-20, lak303d, and warehouse-10-20-10-2-2 for r∈[1,3]r\in[1,3], and analyzed the fraction solved within 60 seconds (success rate) and the length of plan (makespan). Figure 5 shows the empirical result for each setting. The main observation is as follows:

  • •

    Although IU-PIBT works in sparse settings to find a solution, IU-PIBT alone rarely finds a solution in moderately dense situations. This suggests that IU-PIBT alone often gets stuck due to livelocks.

  • •

    LaCAM substantially increases the number of solved instances in dense settings,111Extremely dense scenarios yield too few distance-rr independent sets to sample, so they are outside our experimental scope; consequently, the success rate never falls below 1.01.0 in some settings. indicating that LaCAM resolves stucks by explicitly specifying moves of agents.

  • •

    By explicitly handling livelocks within LaCAM, we further increase the number of solvable instances. This suggests that leveraging the anonymity of agents enables us to plan faster. However, this yields no clear benefit on maps with many narrow corridors (e.g., warehouse-10-20-10-2-2 and r=1r=1), suggesting that there are difficulties other than livelocks in instances on such maps.

7.3 Special case r=0r=0: Unlabeled MAPF

Recall that rrIUMAPF is equivalent to unlabeled MAPF when r=0r=0. Thus, we evaluate the performance of IU-PIBT against existing algorithms specialized in unlabeled MAPF. We carefully choose the state-of-the-art configuration generator-based algorithm TSWAP mapf:tswap as a baseline,222The code is available in https://github.com/Kei18/pytswap.git. and evaluate the running time and solution quality. Both algorithms require an initial target assignment function; we use the Hungarian method. Note that the completeness of the two algorithms does not depend on the assignment function. We use the average running time and the suboptimality of the plan (defined as the plan length over a trivial lower bound) for our evaluation. Here, we use the value of a Bottleneck Matching as the trivial lower bound, as it represents the plan length when each agent moves toward its goal, disregarding any conflicts.

Figure 6 shows the running time and suboptimality in three maps. We observe that the running time does not differ significantly, suggesting that the Hungarian algorithm likely dominates the overall time. However, IU-PIBT achieves lower suboptimality, as it allows more flexible moves than TSWAP.

8 Conclusion

We study rrIUMAPF, a variant of MAPF that introduces an extended collision definition by distance into a standard unlabeled MAPF. This extension makes conventional MAPF algorithms inapplicable, and there are no algorithms readily applicable to rrIUMAPF. We tackle this problem with two approaches from the view of quality and scalability: reduction-based algorithms with compression, and configuration generator-based search. A direction for future work is to develop a search scheme for the unlabeled variant, efficiently handling the anonymity of agents; leave as an open question.

Token Sliding

is a problem that asks whether one can reach a target token placement from a given initial one by moving one token to an adjacent vertex, while maintaining the placement as an independent set reconf:hearn05. Formally, the problem asks whether there exists a sequence of independent sets [S=S0,S1,…,Sℓ=T][S=S_{0},S_{1},\dots,S_{\ell}=T] such that Si−1S_{i-1} and SiS_{i} are adjacent for every i∈[1,ℓ]i\in[1,\ell] under the following rule. In Token Sliding, for two independent sets I1I_{1} and I2I_{2}, we say that I1I_{1} and I2I_{2} are adjacent if there exist vertices u,v∈V​(G)u,v\in V(G) such that I1∖I2={u}I_{1}\setminus I_{2}=\{u\}, I2∖I1={v}I_{2}\setminus I_{1}=\{v\}, and u​v∈E​(G)uv\in E(G). This problem is similar to 11IUMAPF in the sense that we can view agents as tokens and allow at most one token to move to an adjacent vertex in each step. Indeed, some recent works have progressed on settings motivated by MAPF reconf:Kristan25.

It is obvious that Π=[𝒬0,𝒬1,…,𝒬ℓ,𝒬ℓ+1,𝒬ℓ+2]\Pi=[\mathcal{Q}_{0},\mathcal{Q}_{1},...,\mathcal{Q}_{\ell},\mathcal{Q}_{\ell+1},\mathcal{Q}_{\ell+2}] is compatible with Π′\Pi^{\prime}. Moreover, since the agents on planets PP at steps ℓ+1\ell+1 and ℓ+2\ell+2 follow 𝒬k′​[i]\mathcal{Q}_{k}^{\prime}[i], we conclude that 𝒬ℓ+1\mathcal{Q}_{\ell+1} and 𝒬ℓ+2\mathcal{Q}_{\ell+2} are galactic independent. ∎

Next, we discuss the correctness of Reduction rule 2. To this end, we give two lemmas that impose a constraint on plans in G′G^{\prime}.

Lemma 6.

Let Π=[𝒬0,𝒬1,…,𝒬ℓ]\Pi=[\mathcal{Q}_{0},\mathcal{Q}_{1},...,\mathcal{Q}_{\ell}] be a plan from SS to TT for G′G^{\prime}. Then, Π\Pi can be transformed to a plan Π′=[𝒬0′,𝒬1′,…,𝒬ℓ′′]\Pi^{\prime}=[\mathcal{Q}_{0}^{\prime},\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\prime},...,\mathcal{Q}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\prime}] for GG such that no two consecutive configurations have an agent in the neighborhood of bb.

Proof.

Consider a step tt such that 𝒬t∩N​(b)≠∅\mathcal{Q}_{t}\cap N(b)\neq\emptyset. We now give five intermediate configurations 𝒬t1,𝒬t2,𝒬t3,𝒬t4,𝒬t5\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{1},\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{2},\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{3},\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{4},\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{5} between 𝒬t\mathcal{Q}_{t} and 𝒬t+1\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}:

𝒬t1​[i]={b if ​𝒬t​[i]∈N​[b]𝒬t​[i] otherwise\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{1}[i]=\begin{cases}b&\text{ if }\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i]\in N[b]\\ \mathcal{Q}_{t}[i]&\text{ otherwise }\end{cases}
𝒬t2​[i]={b if ​𝒬t​[i]∈N​[b]𝒬t+1​[i] otherwise\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{2}[i]=\begin{cases}b&\text{ if }\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i]\in N[b]\\ \mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i]&\text{ otherwise }\end{cases}
𝒬t3​[i]={b if ​𝒬t​[i]∈N​[b]∨𝒬t+1​[i]∈N​[b]𝒬t+1​[i] otherwise\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{3}[i]=\begin{cases}b&\text{ if }\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i]\in N[b]~\lor~\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i]\in N[b]\\ \mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i]&\text{ otherwise }\end{cases}
𝒬t4​[i]={b if ​𝒬t+1​[i]∈N​[b]𝒬t​[i] otherwise\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{4}[i]=\begin{cases}b&\text{ if }\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i]\in N[b]\\ \mathcal{Q}_{t}[i]&\text{ otherwise }\end{cases}
𝒬t5​[i]={b if ​𝒬t+1​[i]∈N​[b]𝒬t+1​[i] otherwise\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{5}[i]=\begin{cases}b&\text{ if }\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i]\in N[b]\\ \mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i]&\text{ otherwise }\end{cases}

Note that the galactic independence of these five configurations is followed by the galactic independence of 𝒬t\mathcal{Q}_{t} and 𝒬t+1\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}. We claim that the sequence [𝒬t,𝒬t1,𝒬t2,𝒬t3,𝒬t4,𝒬t5,𝒬t+1][\mathcal{Q}_{t},\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{1},\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{2},\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{3},\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{4},\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{5},\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}] is a plan for GG and satisfies the required conditions, that is, no two consecutive configurations have an agent in the neighborhood of bb. For this purpose, we classify the agents into the following four types:

  1. 1.

    𝒬t​[i]∈N​[b]∧𝒬t+1​[i]∈N​[b]\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i]\in N[b]~\land~\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i]\in N[b],

  2. 2.

    𝒬t​[i]∈N​[b]∧𝒬t+1​[i]∉N​[b]\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i]\in N[b]~\land~\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i]\notin N[b],

  3. 3.

    𝒬t​[i]∉N​[b]∧𝒬t+1​[i]∈N​[b]\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i]\notin N[b]~\land~\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i]\in N[b], and

  4. 4.

    𝒬t​[i]∉N​[b]∧𝒬t+1​[i]∉N​[b]\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i]\notin N[b]~\land~\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i]\notin N[b],

and verify their locations in each configuration. For each agent ii, a sequence [𝒬t​[i],𝒬t1​[i],𝒬t2​[i],𝒬t3​[i],𝒬t4​[i],𝒬t5​[i],𝒬t+1​[i]][\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i],\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{1}[i],\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{2}[i],\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{3}[i],\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{4}[i],\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{5}[i],\\ \mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i]] of vertices consists of:
1. [𝒬t​[i],b,b,b,b,b,𝒬t+1​[i]][\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i],b,b,b,b,b,\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i]],
2. [𝒬t​[i],b,b,b,𝒬t​[i],𝒬t+1​[i],𝒬t+1​[i]][\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i],b,b,b,\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i],\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i],\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i]],
3. [𝒬t​[i],𝒬t​[i],𝒬t+1​[i],b,b,b,𝒬t+1​[i]][\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i],\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i],\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i],b,b,b,\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i]], and
4. [𝒬t​[i],𝒬t+1​[i],𝒬t+1​[i],𝒬t+1​[i],𝒬t​[i],𝒬t+1​[i],𝒬t+1​[i]][\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i],\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i],\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i],\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i],\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i],\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i],\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i]].
Thus, every agent either moves to an adjacent vertex along an edge or stays at its current vertex, ensuring the reachability. Moreover, if agent ii is located in a neighbor of bb, it moves out of the open neighborhood of bb in the next step. The lemma follows by applying this procedure to every t∈[0,ℓ−1]t\in[0,\ell-1] such that Qt∩N​(b)≠∅Q_{t}\cap N(b)\neq\emptyset holds. ∎

In what follows, we transform the plan on G′G^{\prime} obtained above into one that satisfies additional restrictions on StproS^{\text{pro}}_{t} and StabsS^{\text{abs}}_{t}.

Lemma 7.

Suppose that G′G^{\prime} is obtained by applying Reduction rule 2 to replace a component CC with a black hole bb. Let Π=[𝒬0,𝒬1,…,𝒬ℓ]\Pi=[\mathcal{Q}_{0},\mathcal{Q}_{1},...,\mathcal{Q}_{\ell}] be a plan for G′G^{\prime} from SS to TT. One can transform it to a plan Π′=[𝒬0′,𝒬1′,…,𝒬ℓ′′]\Pi^{\prime}=[\mathcal{Q}_{0}^{\prime},\mathcal{Q}_{1}^{\prime},...,\mathcal{Q}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\prime}] with the following two conditions:

    no two consecutive configurations of Π′\Pi^{\prime} have an agent in the neighborhood of bb, and

  2. 2.

    |Stpro|+|Stabs|≤1|S^{\text{pro}}_{t}|+|S^{\text{abs}}_{t}|\leq 1 for every t∈[0,ℓ′]t\in[0,\ell^{\prime}].

Proof.

Assume that Π\Pi satisfies condition 1 by applying 6. Consider a step t∈[1,ℓ]t\in[1,\ell] such that |Stpro|+|Stabs|>1|S^{\text{pro}}_{t}|+|S^{\text{abs}}_{t}|>1. Note that it holds that t∉{1,ℓ}t\notin\{1,\ell\} by the fact that b∉N​[S∪T]b\notin N[S\cup T], and |Stpro|=0∨|Stabs|=0|S^{\text{pro}}_{t}|=0\lor|S^{\text{abs}}_{t}|=0 by condition 1. Here, by symmetry, we assume that |Stabs|>0|S^{\text{abs}}_{t}|>0 and |Stpro|=0|S^{\text{pro}}_{t}|=0. Let i1∈Stabsi_{1}\in S^{\text{abs}}_{t} be an agent, and consider the sequence [𝒬t−1,𝒬t−16,𝒬t−17,𝒬t][\mathcal{Q}_{t-1},\mathcal{Q}_{t-1}^{6},\mathcal{Q}_{t-1}^{7},\mathcal{Q}_{t}] with the following:

𝒬t−16​[i]={b if ​i∈Stabs∖{i1}𝒬t−2​[i] otherwise\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}^{6}_{t-1}[i]=\begin{cases}b&\text{ if }i\in S^{\text{abs}}_{t}\setminus\{i_{1}\}\\ \mathcal{Q}_{t-2}[i]&\text{ otherwise }\end{cases}
𝒬t−17​[i]={b if ​i∈Stabs∖{i1}𝒬t−1​[i] otherwise.\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}^{7}_{t-1}[i]=\begin{cases}b&\text{ if }i\in S^{\text{abs}}_{t}\setminus\{i_{1}\}\\ \mathcal{Q}_{t-1}[i]&\text{ otherwise. }\end{cases}

In other words, each agent i∉Stabs∖{i1}i\notin S^{\text{abs}}_{t}\setminus\{i_{1}\} follows the sequence of moves 𝒬t−1​[i]→𝒬t−2​[i]→𝒬t−1​[i]→𝒬t​[i]\mathcal{Q}_{t-1}[i]\to\mathcal{Q}_{t-2}[i]\to\mathcal{Q}_{t-1}[i]\to\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i], and i∈Stabs∖{i1}i\in S^{\text{abs}}_{t}\setminus\{i_{1}\} moves from 𝒬t−1​[i]\mathcal{Q}_{t-1}[i] to b=𝒬t​[i]b=\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i]; hence, this sequence of configurations is a plan for G′G^{\prime}. Moreover, the plan satisfies the condition 1, since 𝒬t−2∩N​(b)=∅\mathcal{Q}_{t-2}\cap N(b)=\emptyset holds from 6.

By inserting this subsequence between 𝒬t−1\mathcal{Q}_{t-1} and 𝒬t\mathcal{Q}_{t}, the size of StabsS^{\text{abs}}_{t} decreases by one. Applying this process iteratively, we eventually achieve |Stabs|=1|S^{\text{abs}}_{t}|=1. We thereby obtain a sequence in which the number of steps satisfying |Stpro|+|Stabs|>1|S^{\text{pro}}_{t}|+|S^{\text{abs}}_{t}|>1 is strictly smaller than that of Π\Pi. Therefore, we can obtain a plan for G′G^{\prime} that satisfies conditions 1 and 2. This completes the proof. ∎

We now demonstrate that Reduction rule 2 is safe using the aforementioned lemmas.

Lemma 8.

Reduction rule 2 is safe.

Proof.

Let G1G_{1} be a graph, and let G2G_{2} be a graph after Reduction rule 2 is applied to a component CC. By 4, if there is a plan from SS to TT for GG, then there is a plan for G′G^{\prime}.

Assume that there is a plan Π=[𝒬0,𝒬1,…,𝒬ℓ]\Pi=[\mathcal{Q}_{0},\mathcal{Q}_{1},...,\mathcal{Q}_{\ell}] for G2G_{2} from SS to TT. By 7, we can assume that Π\Pi satisfies the following two conditions: (i) no two consecutive configurations of Π\Pi have an agent in the neighborhood of bb, and (ii) |Stpro|+|Stabs|≤1|S^{\text{pro}}_{t}|+|S^{\text{abs}}_{t}|\leq 1for every t∈[0,ℓ]t\in[0,\ell]. Consider a vertex v∈Lk∩Cv\in L_{k}\cap C with k≥2​n+3k\geq 2n+3, and a shortest path RR length from vv to a vertex u∈S∪Tu\in S\cup T. Note that for every pair of distance-11 configurations XX and YY in RR with |X|=|Y|≤n|X|=|Y|\leq n, there is a plan from XX to YY that uses only the vertices of RR. Accordingly, for an agent ii that moves to bb at step tt on G2G_{2}, we will instead route ii to a vertex on the path RR on G1G_{1}.

Here, for an agent ii on G2G_{2} and step t′∈[0,ℓ−1]t^{\prime}\in[0,\ell-1], if 𝒬t′​[i]≠b\mathcal{Q}_{t^{\prime}}[i]\neq b and 𝒬t′+1​[i]≠b\mathcal{Q}_{t^{\prime}+1}[i]\neq b, then the same move can be done on G1G_{1}, since G​[V​(G1)∖C]G[V(G_{1})\setminus C] is isomorphic to G​[V​(G2)∖{b}]G[V(G_{2})\setminus\{b\}]. Now we assume that 𝒬t′​[i]=b\mathcal{Q}_{t^{\prime}}[i]=b or 𝒬t′+1​[i]=b\mathcal{Q}_{t^{\prime}+1}[i]=b. Since b∉S∪Tb\notin S\cup T, there is a step t≤t′+1t\leq t^{\prime}+1 such that 𝒬t​[i]∈N​(b)\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i]\in N(b) and 𝒬t+1​[i]=b\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[i]=b. We now show that the agent ii on G1G_{1} can imitate such a move on CC, that is, agent ii can move to some vertex of RR while ensuring that every other agent jj currently contained in CC is also located at some vertex in RR.

Consider shortest paths from 𝒬t​[i]\mathcal{Q}_{t}[i] to every vertex of RR, and let R′R^{\prime} be the shortest one among them. We move agent ii along this path R′R^{\prime} and place it at a vertex r′r^{\prime} on the path RR. Once ii has moved to some vertex of CC, for each agent j≠ij\neq i contained in N​[C]∖CN[C]\setminus C, we move it to 𝒬t+1​[j]\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[j]. This ensures that ii and jj are never on adjacent vertices, since 𝒬t+1​[j]∉N​[b]\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}[j]\notin N[b] on G2G_{2}, and thus 𝒬t+1′​[j]∉N​[C]\mathcal{Q}_{t+1}^{\prime}[j]\notin N[C] on G1G_{1}. Before ii reaches the endpoint r′r^{\prime}, agent ii could become adjacent to an agent kk on RR, violating the independence. In this case, ii is at the vertex v′v^{\prime} on R′R^{\prime} adjacent to r′r^{\prime}. Note that N​(v′)∩RN(v^{\prime})\cap R consists of at most three consecutive vertices on RR; otherwise, we would obtain a path shorter than RR via v′v^{\prime}. Accordingly, we ensure that no agent is placed on N​(v′)∩RN(v^{\prime})\cap R before agent ii moves to v′v^{\prime}. Here, after removing at most three vertices in N​(v′)∩RN(v^{\prime})\cap R from RR, there remain at least 2​n−22n-2 vertices, which can accommodate an independent set of size n−1n-1. Then, we move the agents on RR so that they form this independent set. After completing these moves, agent ii can move from v′v^{\prime} to r′r^{\prime}. Therefore, the agent ii on G1G_{1} can imitate a move on G2G_{2} from a vertex in N​(b)N(b) to bb.

Until agent ii moves from bb to a vertex in N​(b)N(b) on G2G_{2}, it can be kept at some vertex of RR. This holds because, whenever another agent jj moves to bb, agent jj can imitate its move on G2G_{2}.

From here on, we consider the reverse move, that is, ii moves from bb to a vertex in v∈N​(b)v\in N(b) at step t1t_{1}. we try to move ii from a vertex on RR to v∈N​(b)v\in N(b). However, since there may be other agents on RR, it might be impossible to move ii without violating the independence constraint. Nevertheless, by considering the shortest path R′R^{\prime} from vv to a vertex RR again, we can see that at least one agent jj can be moved to vv. Then, consider the sequence obtained by swapping 𝒬t′​[i]\mathcal{Q}_{t^{\prime}}[i] and 𝒬t′​[j]\mathcal{Q}_{t^{\prime}}[j] in every configuration 𝒬t′\mathcal{Q}_{t^{\prime}} with t′≥t1t^{\prime}\geq t_{1}. This sequence is also a plan from SS to TT on G2G_{2}, and it yields a sequence in which jj moves to vv on G1G_{1}. Here, every agent ii holds that 𝒬ℓ​[i]∉N​[b]\mathcal{Q}_{\ell}[i]\notin N[b], since b∉N​[T]b\notin N[T]. Eventually, every agent moves from bb to some planet. At some step, agent ii can imitate the move of some agent moving from bb to N​(b)N(b). This completes the proof. ∎

5 and 8 immediately lead to 1.

We bound the running time to obtain an instance after applying Reduction rules 1 and 2 until no updates are possible. We first compute the layers in time O​(|V​(G)|+|E​(G)|)O(|V(G)|+|E(G)|) using Breadth-first search. Reduction rule 1 searches for adjacent black holds and Reduction rule 2 contract a component to a vertex. Thus, each application of the rules requires O​(|V​(G)|+|E​(G)|)O(|V(G)|+|E(G)|) time. The running time is O​(|V​(G)|+|E​(G)|)O(|V(G)|+|E(G)|).

We now provide an upper bound on the size of the obtained instance. We first claim that the size of BB is bounded by Δ⋅|P|\Delta\cdot|P|. Since there is no edge b1​b2∈Bb_{1}b_{2}\in B such that b1,b2b_{1},b_{2} are both in BB, the remaining black hole b∈Bb\in B holds that N​(b)⊆PN(b)\subseteq P. Moreover, we can see that the degree of vertex v∈Pv\in P does not increase by applying Reduction rules 1 and 2. Thus, |B||B| can be upper bounded by |N​[P]|≤Δ​|P||N[P]|\leq\Delta|P|. It remains only to bound |P||P|.

∑0≤k≤2​n+2|Lk|\displaystyle\sum_{0\leq k\leq 2n+2}|L_{k}|

Here, when an induced grid graph is given, the above bound is overestimated. Any vertex within distance kk from a vertex vv lies inside the grid of width 2​k2k centered at vv. Thus, ∑0≤k≤2​n+2|Lk|=O​(|S∪T|⋅n2)=O​(n3)\sum_{0\leq k\leq 2n+2}|L_{k}|=O(|S\cup T|\cdot n^{2})=O(n^{3}). This leads to the following theorem.

Proof.

Let (G,S,T)(G,S,T) be an instance of 1​IUMAPF{1{\textsc{IUMAPF}}}. We transform it to an instance (G′,S,T)(G^{\prime},S,T) of GMAPF, where a set of planets is V​(G)V(G) and a set of black holes is ∅\emptyset. Remark.

We note that the lemma established above does not specialize to GMAPF and also applies to Galactic Token Sliding, a galactic variant of Token Sliding. Therefore, we can say that Galactic Token Sliding admits a kernel with ΔO​(n)​n\Delta^{O(n)}n vertices in general, and with O​(n3)O(n^{3}) vertices when an induced grid graph is given. This claim improves the known upper bound on the kernel size ΔO​(n2)​n\Delta^{O(n^{2})}n in gal:Bartier23.

Proof.

We show that IU-LaCAM can generate all reachable configurations for every configuration 𝒬\mathcal{Q} in finite time. This leads to the fact that, for every vertex subset TT such that there is a plan from SS to TT, a plan from SS to TT can be obtained by traversing a generated reachable configuration from SS, implying the completeness, since the number of configurations is bounded by 2|V​(G)|2^{|V(G)|}.

We proceed to prove the initial claim. To this end, we prove the following: (i) the number of node reinserts (in line 10) is bounded, and (ii) the number of possible constraints are bounded.

For (i), we show that ∑i∈A|ℬ​[i]|\sum_{i\in A}|\mathcal{B}[i]| is strictly increases when if-statement in line 5 is true. It is clear that DD is not empty; otherwise 𝒬=T\mathcal{Q}=T, thus a plan from SS to TT is already obtained. Therefore, there is an agent such that |ℬ​[i]||\mathcal{B}[i]| increases, derives that ∑i∈A|ℬ​[i]|\sum_{i\in A}|\mathcal{B}[i]| increases. The upper bound of ∑i∈A|ℬ​[i]|\sum_{i\in A}|\mathcal{B}[i]| is |A|2|A|^{2}, thus the number of node reinserts is also bounded by |A|2|A|^{2}.

Next, for (ii), constraints have information that includes a subset of agents and their next locations. Here, the number of subsets of agents is bounded by 2|A|2^{|A|}, and the number of candidate next locations is bounded by Δ+1\Delta+1 for each agent. Thus, the number of constraints is bounded by 2|A|⋅(Δ+1)|A|2^{|A|}\cdot(\Delta+1)^{|A|}.

We show that IU-LaCAM can generate all reachable configurations for every configuration 𝒬\mathcal{Q} in finite time. This completes the proof. ∎
